meta.label: Rugby Union
meta.contactLevel: very high (tackles, rucks, mauls, scrums) — the defining physical feature of the sport
meta.competitionFrequencyPerWeek: 1 match/week typical; 2 matches/week in congested professional blocks and cup rounds
meta.notes: Two 40-minute halves of intermittent running punctuated by repeated maximal collisions — tackles, rucks, mauls and scrums. Ball-in-play is only ~35 minutes but the collision count (20-40+ contacts for a forward) is the load that defines the sport. The gym's job here is unusually central: it builds the maximal strength and neck/shoulder robustness that let a player survive and dominate contact, then supports acceleration and repeat-effort capacity. Unlike soccer, rugby IS a strength sport — heavy lifting is sport-specific, not a supplement. Collision load and head-impact exposure make neck strengthening and criteria-based concussion management non-negotiable.

maxStrength.why: Scrum drive, maul push, tackle dominance and contact tolerance are all maximal-force expressions; stronger players win collisions and get injured less. Rugby is genuinely strength-limited in a way most field sports are not.
maxStrength.source: Duthie 2003 (applied physiology of rugby union review); Argus 2012 (strength/power in professional rugby)

explosivePower.why: The rate of force into contact decides tackles and ball-carries; jumping (lineout/restart), driving off the mark and the first hit all express rapid force. Power correlates with playing level in professional rugby.

neckStrength.why: Scrummaging transmits enormous compressive/shear load through the cervical spine, and neck strength is a modifiable factor plausibly attenuating head accelerations in tackles — relevant to concussion and catastrophic neck-injury risk. World Rugby prioritises cervical conditioning for front-row eligibility.
neckStrength.source: Hrysomallis 2016 (neck muscular strength, training and concussion risk review); World Rugby scrum/front-row conditioning guidance

collisionRobustness.why: Tolerating 20-40+ maximal contacts per match without tissue failure or performance decay is the sport's signature demand; it is built from maximal strength, lean mass, trunk stiffness and specific contact conditioning.

acceleration.why: Most rugby sprints are short (<20 m) from a static or moving start — hitting the line, chasing kicks, defensive line-speed; the first three steps create and deny contact.

repeatSprintAbility.why: Repeated high-intensity efforts (sprints AND collisions) with incomplete recovery across 80 minutes; the decisive phases cluster in multi-phase attack and scramble defence.
repeatSprintAbility.source: Duthie 2003; Austin 2011 (repeated high-intensity exercise in professional rugby)

strengthEndurance.why: Back-row and front-row work is repeated near-maximal grappling — rucks, mauls, scrums, tackles — demanding the ability to reproduce force under accumulating fatigue, not just a single peak.

sprintSpeed.why: Outside backs reach near-maximal velocity on breaks, chases and cover-defence; top-end speed separates line-breakers and exposes the hamstring to the same eccentric load that injures it.

aerobicEndurance.why: Underpins repeated-effort recovery across 80 minutes and protects late-match tackle technique and decision-making; the aerobic base lets the anaerobic system reload between collisions.

deceleration.why: Defensive line-speed then braking to make a square tackle, and change of contact angle, demand high eccentric capacity — the tissue armour for hamstring and knee.
deceleration.source: Harper 2019 (deceleration demands in team sport); expert consensus

changeOfDirection.why: Evasion (step, swerve, fend) in attack and re-alignment in defence; sharp COD creates half-breaks and is a knee-loading mechanism to be trained deliberately.

relativeStrength.why: Strength-to-bodyweight drives acceleration and evasion for backs and mobile forwards; mass must be functional, not carried dead weight over repeated sprints.

reactiveStrength.why: Stiffness for re-acceleration, restart/lineout jump-land and repeated ground contacts; a targeted dose also underpins protective landing mechanics.

aerialAbility.why: Lineout jumping and lifting, restart contests and high-ball reclaims; decisive for locks, back-row jumpers and back-three players under the high ball.

rotationalPower.why: Passing (especially the scrum-half pass and long spin), fending and rotating in contact express trunk power; useful but secondary to bracing.

mobility.why: Hip and thoracic range for scrummaging body position, ruck clear-outs and safe tackle height; restricted range pushes load into the lumbar spine.

coordination.why: Handling, offloading and decision-making under fatigue and contact define quality; gym work must never arrive fatigued enough to blunt skill execution.

gripStrength.why: Ball security in contact, tackle completion (holding and dragging) and lineout lifting all draw on grip and forearm strength; higher demand than most field sports.

energySystems.workToRestRatio: intermittent — brief maximal efforts (sprints, collisions) on ~1:5 to 1:15 work:rest embedded in near-continuous low-intensity activity; forwards higher work density than backs
energySystems.matchDemands: ~5-7 km total (forwards lower, backs higher); ~35 min ball-in-play; 20-40+ contacts for a forward, fewer but higher-speed for backs; repeated static exertions (scrums, mauls, rucks) add a large isometric/collision load invisible to distance metrics
energySystems.heartRateProfile: Intermittent high — sustained periods >85% HRmax with collision-driven spikes; blood lactate rises sharply through set-piece and multi-phase play
energySystems.fatigueProfile: Collision fatigue compounds running fatigue — tackle technique, sprint output and cognitive accuracy degrade late; neuromuscular and tissue recovery from a match is slow (48-72+ h) because of the eccentric/impact component
energySystems.source: Duthie 2003 (applied physiology review); Austin 2011 (repeated high-intensity exercise); position splits are elite estimates
energySystems.notes: Position-dependent: forwards accumulate collision/static load at lower running distance; backs cover more ground at higher speed. The gym supplies the maximal strength and robustness the pitch cannot safely dose, plus targeted power and repeat-effort support.

primaryPatterns: scrum/maul drive (sustained horizontal push from a braced spine)
ruck clear-out and lift (explosive hip extension + trunk stiffness)
change of direction / evasion (step, swerve, fend)
movementProfile.jointLoading: High axial/compressive load through the spine in scrum and contact; high eccentric hamstring load in top-speed running (backs); shoulder and AC-joint loading in tackling; cervical-spine load in scrummaging and tackle; knee valgus/rotation exposure in evasion and contact
movementProfile.groundContacts: Moderate running volume plus a very high count of impact/collision contacts; the collision count, not the running distance, is the defining load
movementProfile.landingDemands: High for jumpers/lifters (lineout, restart) and for any player brought to ground in contact; safe fall/land mechanics matter
movementProfile.throwing: Lineout throw (hooker) and passing (all — scrum-half most); moderate programming relevance for the throwing shoulder and trunk
movementProfile.jumping: High for locks and back-row jumpers (lineout, restart); moderate for back-three contesting the high ball
movementProfile.cutting: Frequent in attack (evasion) and defence (re-alignment); a knee-loading mechanism to prepare
movementProfile.rotating: Fending, passing and rotating out of contact load the trunk in rotation; bracing capacity comes first
movementProfile.overheadActions: Lineout lifting and jumping load the overhead/shoulder position under a partner's bodyweight; shoulder robustness is a real programming target
movementProfile.collisions: The defining demand — repeated maximal tackles, rucks, mauls and scrums; the single largest driver of injury and recovery cost
movementProfile.repeatedImpacts: High cumulative contact and ground-impact load; head-impact exposure accumulates and is managed as its own risk stream
movementProfile.asymmetricLoading: Tackle-shoulder preference, scrum-bind side and kicking-leg dominance create side-specific loading that must be audited
commonDeficiencies: cervical (neck) strength vs scrum + tackle + head-impact exposure (the sport-specific under-trained quality)
eccentric hamstring strength vs top-speed running (backs) and re-acceleration
shoulder/rotator-cuff robustness vs tackle and lineout-lift load
trunk anti-extension/anti-rotation stiffness for contact and spine protection
posterior-chain maximal strength vs scrum/maul drive

common.name: Concussion / head injury
common.incidence: very high — the single most commonly reported match injury in professional rugby union and rising in reporting; the sport's headline health priority
common.severity: variable — days to weeks (graduated return-to-play), with serious concern over cumulative exposure and long-term brain health
common.mechanism: tackle events dominate — both the ball-carrier and (more often) the tackler; head contact with an opponent, the ground or a knee/hip

modifiable: neck strength (modifiable factor — plausibly attenuates head acceleration)

common.rtpConsiderations: Governed by the World Rugby Graduated Return-To-Play protocol — NOT a criteria-the-coach-decides call. Symptom-free progression through stages; strength/conditioning resumes only within the protocol. The gym's contribution is upstream: cervical strengthening as a modifiable risk factor, never a treatment.
common.source: Williams 2013 (systematic review of rugby union injuries); World Rugby GRTP protocol; Hrysomallis 2016 (neck strength as a modifiable factor)

common.name: Shoulder instability / dislocation & AC-joint injury
common.incidence: high — shoulder is among the most common and highest-burden injury regions; tackling is the primary event
common.severity: moderate-severe — dislocations and labral/AC injuries are often long lay-offs and can be surgical and recurrence-prone
common.mechanism: tackling (both roles), direct fall onto the point of the shoulder, and forced abduction/external rotation in contact
common.rtpConsiderations: Criteria-based: restore cuff/scapular strength symmetry and range, then graded contact reintroduction (tackle bag → controlled live). Recurrent instability often needs surgical stabilisation before contact return.
common.source: Williams 2013; Headey 2007 (shoulder injuries in professional rugby)

common.name: Hamstring strain
common.incidence: high — the most common muscle injury, concentrated in backs and mobile forwards
common.mechanism: high-speed running — eccentric overload at terminal swing; re-acceleration and kick-chase efforts

modifiable: inadequate or spiked high-speed running exposure

common.rtpConsiderations: Criteria-based: restore eccentric strength symmetry (Nordic), then progressive sprint reloading to >95% max velocity BEFORE match return; unreloaded returns drive recurrence.
common.source: Brooks 2006 (hamstring injuries in English professional rugby); Attwood 2018 (efficacy of a movement-control programme); van Dyk 2019 (Nordic meta-analysis)

common.name: Ankle syndesmosis (high ankle) & lateral sprain
common.incidence: high — ankle is a common joint injury; syndesmosis (high) sprains are frequent in rucks/mauls and carry long lay-offs
common.severity: lateral sprain low-moderate; syndesmosis moderate-severe (often 6+ weeks) and recurrence-prone
common.mechanism: external rotation of a loaded, planted foot in rucks/mauls and being fallen on (syndesmosis); inversion under contact and in cutting (lateral)

modifiable: incomplete rehab of a prior sprain

common.rtpConsiderations: Syndesmosis needs conservative, criteria-based loading progression and often longer than a lateral sprain; graded COD and contact re-exposure with balance retraining; bracing/taping on return.
common.source: Williams 2013; Fuller 2007 (Rugby World Cup injury surveillance)

common.name: Knee ligament injury (MCL / ACL)
common.incidence: moderate frequency but the highest-burden lower-limb injury (longest lay-offs)
common.severity: MCL moderate; ACL severe — season-ending (6-12 months) and recurrence-prone
common.mechanism: contact valgus load in the tackle (MCL) and plant-and-cut or single-leg landing with valgus/rotation, often perturbed in contact (ACL, ~contact and non-contact mix)
common.rtpConsiderations: Criteria-based and time-respecting for ACL (≥9 months lowers re-injury): strength symmetry, hop battery, on-pitch COD then graded contact, psychological readiness.
common.source: Williams 2013; Dallalana 2007 (knee injuries in professional rugby)

common.name: Lumbar spine / lower-back injury
common.incidence: moderate — chronic and acute low-back complaints are common in forwards from repeated scrummaging and contact loading
common.severity: variable — nagging and recurrence-prone; can cause missed training more than missed matches
common.mechanism: repeated flexion/compression and shear in scrummaging, mauling and lifting; acute loading in poorly braced contact

modifiable: hip and thoracic mobility restriction pushing load into the lumbar spine
excessive spinal loading volume without recovery

common.rtpConsiderations: Build trunk stiffness and hip/thoracic range; manage axial-loading volume; graded return to scrummaging; avoid heavy loaded flexion.
common.source: Williams 2013; expert consensus (rugby S&C on axial load management)

injuryProfile.summary: Rugby's injury profile is dominated by CONTACT: concussion is the headline health priority (managed by the World Rugby GRTP protocol, not by the coach), shoulder and knee injuries carry the highest burden, and the tackle is the single event behind most of them. Muscle strains (hamstring) and ankle syndesmosis add to the load. The gym owns real, upstream contributions — maximal strength and lean mass for contact tolerance, cervical strengthening as a modifiable concussion-risk factor (Hrysomallis 2016), rotator-cuff/scapular robustness for the shoulder, Nordic eccentric work for the hamstring, and trunk stiffness for the spine. Availability is the transfer: injury burden predicts team success, and the tackle is where most of it is won or lost.

positions.name: Front row (props & hooker)
positions.role: Scrum engine, close-quarter contact, ruck/maul work, lineout throwing (hooker) and lifting; the heaviest collision and axial-load workload in the team.
positions.movementDemands: Sustained maximal scrum drive, repeated rucking and mauling, short hard accelerations into contact; lowest running distance, highest static/collision load.
positions.runningDemands: Lowest total distance (~5-6 km), almost all low-speed; very high collision and isometric load.
positions.collisionDemands: Highest — scrums, close-in carries and cleanouts every phase.
positions.powerReq: high (scrum drive off the mark, cleanout)
positions.strengthReq: very high (maximal scrum and contact force; the strongest players on the pitch)
positions.bodyComposition: Heaviest, most powerful build; high lean mass with enough conditioning for repeated set-piece.
gymPriorities: cervical strengthening — non-negotiable for front-row eligibility and safety
trunk anti-extension/anti-rotation stiffness for spine protection
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Very high collision + axial load; heavy spinal-loading gym work must be spaced from scrum-heavy pitch sessions and matches; neck work is a permanent weekly fixture.

positions.name: Second row (locks)
positions.role: Lineout jumping and lifting, restart contests, scrum drive, high-volume ruck/maul work; the aerial and engine forwards.
positions.movementDemands: Repeated maximal jumps and lifts, sustained scrum/maul drive, continuous rucking; large frame moved over ~6-7 km.
positions.runningDemands: Low-moderate (~6-7 km); high work density in tight play.
positions.collisionDemands: Very high — set-piece, cleanout and carry volume.
positions.strengthReq: very high (scrum, maul, lift under a partner's load)
positions.bodyComposition: Tallest players; long levers with high strength and lean mass.
gymPriorities: shoulder + scapular robustness for lifting overhead under load
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Jump-land and lift load plus collision; manage overhead shoulder volume and axial loading; neck micro-dose weekly.

positions.name: Back row (flankers & No. 8)
positions.role: The link forwards — tackling, jackaling, carrying, covering; the highest repeat-effort workload in the pack, blending collision with ground coverage.
positions.movementDemands: Repeated high-intensity efforts — tackle, get up, sprint to the next ruck, carry, repeat; the densest collision-plus-running load in the team.
positions.runningDemands: Highest of the forwards (~7 km) at a high work:rest density.
positions.collisionDemands: Very high — the most tackles and cleanouts of any position group.
positions.bodyComposition: Powerful but mobile — the athletic all-round forward build.
gymPriorities: rotator-cuff/scapular + neck robustness for high tackle volume
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest combined collision + running load; the gym flexes hard around their pitch load in-season; prevention pillars are protective, not optional.

positions.name: Half-backs (scrum-half & fly-half)
positions.role: The controllers — service and distribution, tactical kicking, decision-making, defensive organisation; high skill under fatigue and contact.
positions.movementDemands: Constant short movement, repeated passing (scrum-half) and kicking (fly-half), sharp acceleration and evasion; high cognitive load with contact exposure at the ruck and in defence.
positions.runningDemands: Moderate (~6-7 km) with frequent short accelerations and direction changes.
positions.collisionDemands: Moderate — smaller frames but exposed to tackling and the ruck.
positions.bodyComposition: Lean, fast and durable; strength for contact without carrying excess mass.
gymPriorities: acceleration strength (hip thrust, sled, split squat)
trunk anti-rotation + rotational power for passing and kicking
single-leg strength and eccentric hamstring for repeated acceleration
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Skill quality is the job — gym work must arrive fresh enough never to blunt passing and kicking; count kicking volume (fly-half) as load.

positions.name: Outside backs (wings, fullback, centres)
positions.role: Finishing and covering — top-speed line-breaks, kick-chase and counter, high-ball contests and last-line defence; the fastest players with the highest sprint exposure.
positions.movementDemands: Maximal-velocity sprints on breaks, chases and cover; repeated high-ball jump-land; hard collisions in the tackle and midfield contact (centres).
positions.runningDemands: Highest total and high-speed distance (~7 km, top-end speed exposure peaks here).
positions.collisionDemands: High for centres (midfield contact), moderate-high for wings/fullback (finishing and covering).
positions.speedReq: very high (top-end velocity wins and saves tries)
positions.bodyComposition: Fast-powerful; centres carry more mass, wings/fullback leaner and faster.
commonInjuries: hamstring (highest top-speed exposure in the team)
gymPriorities: eccentric hamstring capacity (Nordic) — non-negotiable at this sprint exposure
max-velocity support (heavy strength + sprint exposure on pitch)
landing mechanics + neck robustness for aerial contests
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest weekly max-velocity load — heavy posterior-chain gym work needs 48 h separation from sprint-dense sessions and matches.

assessments.name: 1RM (or 3-5RM est.) back squat / trap-bar deadlift
assessments.purpose: Global maximal-strength anchor — the quality that most directly drives scrum drive, contact dominance and acceleration in rugby.

assessments.name: Countermovement jump (CMJ)
assessments.purpose: Lower-body power benchmark + weekly neuromuscular-fatigue monitor (drop vs rolling baseline), especially valuable given rugby's slow post-collision recovery.

assessments.name: Isometric neck strength (multi-direction)
assessments.purpose: Cervical strength benchmark and symmetry check — a modifiable factor for concussion and neck-injury risk, and a front-row safety requirement.

targets.elite: high, symmetrical flexion/extension/lateral force vs position norms (front row highest)

assessments.source: Hrysomallis 2016 (neck strength and concussion review); Naish 2013 (neck strength in rugby players)

assessments.name: 10 m / 40 m sprint
assessments.purpose: Acceleration (10 m) is the game's decisive short action; 40 m captures near-maximal velocity, the hamstring-relevant exposure for backs.

targets.elite: 10 m ~1.7-1.8 s; 40 m ~5.0-5.3 s (backs, male professional)

assessments.name: Bronco test (or Yo-Yo IR1)
assessments.purpose: Repeated high-intensity running capacity — the rugby conditioning benchmark (Bronco is the rugby-specific shuttle; Yo-Yo IR1 is the validated intermittent alternative).

targets.elite: Bronco ~4:20-5:00 (backs faster than forwards); Yo-Yo IR1 ≥1800-2200 m

assessments.name: Nordic hamstring strength
assessments.purpose: Eccentric hamstring strength — the headline modifiable factor for rugby's most common muscle injury, especially in backs.
assessments.frequency: each block + after any hamstring flag

targets.elite: high force + symmetrical (<10% imbalance); full-control Nordic

assessments.name: 1RM bench press (or 3-5RM est.)
assessments.purpose: Upper-body pressing strength anchor — relevant to fending, contact and lineout lifting; a standard rugby strength benchmark.

assessments.name: Repeated-effort / repeat-sprint battery
assessments.purpose: Sprint (and, ideally, collision) decrement under incomplete recovery — the repeated-high-intensity quality that defines back-row and midfield work.
assessments.source: Austin 2011 (repeated high-intensity exercise in professional rugby)

highest: movement literacy + sprint and landing mechanics
bodyweight strength (squat, hinge, push, pull, brace, fall/land)
SAFE contact and tackle technique BEFORE contact volume
multi-sport exposure
youth.trainingEmphasis: Athletic literacy and safe contact technique first; introduce cervical conditioning early and lightly given the collision future. Growth-spurt years need patience with load. World Rugby Activate-style neuromuscular warm-ups are proven and free.
commonMistakes: adding contact volume before contact SKILL is safe
neglecting neck and landing preparation in a collision sport

highest: maximal-strength base (the rugby foundation) with sound technique
eccentric hamstring habit (Nordic) BEFORE senior sprint + contact volumes
cervical + shoulder robustness base
trunk stiffness and hip/thoracic mobility
lowest: maximal contact conditioning before a strength base exists
development.trainingEmphasis: Build the strength and robustness the senior game will tax — a real strength base is the entry ticket to safe senior contact. Prevention pillars (Nordic, neck, shoulder) become permanent habits here.
commonMistakes: skills-and-contact only with no strength base
senior contact loads without robustness preparation
no neck/shoulder base before front-row or back-row demands

highest: maximal strength + power development and maintenance
availability: Nordic + neck + shoulder prehab every week
repeat-effort and acceleration quality
readiness-led load management around collisions and fixtures
senior.trainingEmphasis: Rugby rewards strength — keep developing it, but protect the match: gym work flexes around collision load and fixture congestion, never compounds them. Neck and shoulder prehab are weekly non-negotiables.
commonMistakes: stacking heavy gym volume on top of a high-collision week
dropping prehab pillars when fixtures compress (when risk peaks)
treating post-match recovery like a lower-collision sport (rugby recovery is slower)

highest: individualised limiter work (data-led, position-specific)
strength/power maintenance through congestion and heavy collision load
squad-level rotation + collision-load planning
criteria-based rehab pathways (and GRTP for head injury)
elite.trainingEmphasis: Individualised, monitored development around a long collision-heavy calendar; the physical programme is availability + contact-dominance management.
commonMistakes: copying another player's or position's programme
returning players to contact without robustness and (for head injury) GRTP completion

highest: strength/power retention
neck, shoulder and tendon care (the collision-veteran profile)
mobility upkeep
longer recovery cycles between matches
masters.trainingEmphasis: Retain strength and robustness; respect a slower recovery curve and the accumulated contact history; manage collision exposure deliberately.
commonMistakes: high contact volume without a maintained strength base

offSeason.primaryObjective: Rebuild maximal strength, lean mass, and neck/shoulder/hamstring robustness; fix the season's asymmetries and carried niggles; rebuild aerobic base.
offSeason.trainingEmphasis: Max strength + targeted hypertrophy (position-specific mass); eccentric robustness at full dose (the soreness window nobody minds); cervical and shoulder base-building; aerobic base.
offSeason.fatigueTolerance: high (no matches or collisions to protect)

programming.source: rugby S&C: off-season rounds out + hypertrophy/mass base; in-season maintains max-strength + collision robustness at minimal effective volume

preSeason.primaryObjective: Convert strength to power and acceleration; rebuild collision conditioning and high-speed-running tolerance progressively; reach match fitness without a pre-season injury spike.
preSeason.trainingEmphasis: Power + speed conversion; progressive contact conditioning and sprint exposure to >95% max velocity; Nordic/neck/shoulder doses established before contact volume ramps.
preSeason.recoveryEmphasis: moderate-high (contact + running load rising fast — a high-risk ACWR window)
testingRecommendations: CMJ + neck-strength baseline for the season

programming.source: rugby S&C: off-season rounds out + hypertrophy/mass base; in-season maintains max-strength + collision robustness at minimal effective volume

competition.primaryObjective: Maintain strength, power and robustness at minimal effective volume; maximise availability across a collision-heavy ~36-week season.
competition.trainingEmphasis: 1-2 heavy-but-low-volume sessions anchored to match day (MD-4/MD-3); neck + shoulder + hamstring prehab EVERY week; power micro-doses MD-2.
competition.fatigueTolerance: low (protect the player from compounding collision load)
testingRecommendations: weekly CMJ monitoring; periodic neck-strength check

programming.source: rugby S&C: off-season rounds out + hypertrophy/mass base; in-season maintains max-strength + collision robustness at minimal effective volume

playoffs.primaryObjective: Peak freshness + availability for finals; the collision cost of the run-in is already high.
playoffs.trainingEmphasis: Minimal-volume high-intensity maintenance; match-day priming; ruthless prioritisation of prehab pillars.

recovery.primaryObjective: Physical and mental recovery after a long collision season; restore tissue; treat carried niggles.
recovery.trainingEmphasis: 2+ weeks genuinely off contact, then unstructured activity, mobility, light cross-training; rehab the season's flags before off-season loading starts.

oneMatchPerWeek.pattern: MD-anchored week: recover from collision load, load heavy far from the match, sharpen close to it.
oneMatchPerWeek.heavyDay: MD-4 or MD-3 (maximal lower + upper strength; furthest from both matches — collision recovery permitting)
oneMatchPerWeek.recoveryDay: MD+1 and MD+2 (active recovery + mobility; collision recovery is slower than in non-contact sport)
oneMatchPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: neck + shoulder + hamstring prehab MD-4/MD-3 (and a short neck top-up MD-2); never a first heavy eccentric exposure inside MD-2
oneMatchPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: MD+1/+2 recovery → MD-4 high (gym heavy + prehab) → MD-3 moderate → MD-2 power/speed + priming → MD-1 light → MD

twoMatchesPerWeek.pattern: Congested block: recovery-first, maintenance micro-doses only between matches — the collision load makes this stricter than for non-contact sports.
twoMatchesPerWeek.powerDay: optional priming micro-dose only if >72 h between matches
twoMatchesPerWeek.recoveryDay: the day(s) after each match (collision recovery dominates)
twoMatchesPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: low-dose maintenance only (neck isometrics, short-lever prehab, hamstring isometrics)
twoMatchesPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Match → recovery → recovery/priming → Match → recovery; cut gym volume ~50%; rotate squad where possible.

tournamentOrCongested.pattern: Tournament rugby (cup weeks, 3 matches in ~9-10 days) = pure availability + collision-load management.
tournamentOrCongested.injuryPreventionDay: minimal-dose isometrics (neck holds, hamstring holds, trunk holds)
tournamentOrCongested.typicalLoadingPattern: Protect recovery between fixtures; gym is priming, never development; injury risk concentrates in the later fixtures as collision fatigue accumulates.

transfersWell: heavy bilateral + single-leg strength (squat, trap-bar, split squat — the direct scrum/contact/acceleration currency)
posterior-chain strength (RDL, hip thrust — scrum drive, sprint, contact)
eccentric hamstring work (Nordic, GHR) — the hamstring armour for backs and mobile forwards
cervical (neck) strengthening — the sport-specific under-trained modifiable risk factor
rotator-cuff + scapular robustness (tackle + lineout-lift shoulder protection)
Olympic-lift derivatives / triple-extension power (rate of force into contact and off the mark)
anti-extension + anti-rotation trunk work (spine protection in contact and scrum)
loaded carries + grip work (ball security, tackle completion, lift)
limitedValue: bodybuilding-volume isolation work with no contact or performance currency
long steady-state gym cardio (the pitch + conditioning already supply it)
loaded spinal flexion volume (sit-ups) — adds lumbar risk a brace does not
chasing hypertrophy past the point mass costs repeat-effort speed
accessoryPriorities: neck isometrics (all positions, front row highest)
rotator-cuff + scapular work (face pulls, external rotation)
gymPhilosophy.singleLegEmphasis: High — acceleration, evasion and many contact events are single-leg; single-leg strength complements (never replaces) the heavy bilateral base that scrummaging demands.
gymPhilosophy.olympicLiftingSuitability: High value where technique allows — cleans and derivatives train the rate of force development that rugby contact rewards; trap-bar jumps, hang high-pulls and mid-thigh pulls deliver most of the benefit at lower technical cost and are easier to keep in-season.
gymPhilosophy.plyometricEmphasis: Moderate and targeted: landing mechanics, low-dose reactive stiffness, and jump-land/lift for locks and back-row; the game already supplies large reactive and impact volume.
gymPhilosophy.coreTrainingPhilosophy: The trunk is a stiff transmitter and protector: anti-extension and anti-rotation strength for contact, scrum and spine protection first; rotational power (pass/fend) second. No loaded-flexion volume.
gymPhilosophy.neckTraining: HIGH priority — unlike most field sports, cervical strengthening is a weekly non-negotiable: multi-direction isometrics for all positions (front row highest), as a modifiable factor for concussion and neck-injury risk and a front-row safety requirement.
gymPhilosophy.gripTraining: Moderate priority — ball security in contact, tackle completion and lineout lifting draw on grip; loaded carries cover most of the need.
gymPhilosophy.rotationalTraining: Moderate — anti-rotation bracing first, then low-dose rotational power for passing, fending and kicking (half-backs and backs).
gymPhilosophy.isometricTraining: Valuable in-season and in congestion: neck isometrics, hamstring isometrics and trunk holds maintain capacity at minimal soreness cost when collision load is high.
gymPhilosophy.tempoRecommendations: Controlled eccentrics in robustness phases (hamstring, neck, cuff); explosive intent on all power and strength-speed work.
gymPhilosophy.velocityRecommendations: Heavy-fast intent for maximal strength and strength-speed; light-load maximal-intent jumps, cleans and sled work for the power/acceleration profile; sprinting and contact conditioning stay on the pitch, programmed and counted.

warningSigns: any head-contact event with symptoms — headache, fog, balance change
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: cervical strengthening 2-3x/week year-round (all positions; front row highest); tackle-technique coaching is the primary prevention
exercisesToAvoid: return to contact before completing the World Rugby GRTP protocol
monitoringRecommendations: strict adherence to the World Rugby Graduated Return-To-Play protocol (clinician-led, NOT a coaching decision)
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Hrysomallis 2016 (neck strength as a modifiable factor); Williams 2013 (epidemiology); World Rugby GRTP protocol

riskFactors: high tackle volume without contact conditioning
warningSigns: apprehension or laxity at end range
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: cuff + scapular robustness 2-3x/week; heavy pulling strength in the strength block; graded contact conditioning before contact volume
exercisesToAvoid: provocative end-range loading on a symptomatic/unstable shoulder
high contact volume before cuff strength + range are restored
monitoringRecommendations: range and apprehension check after any shoulder event
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Headey 2007 (shoulder injuries in professional rugby); Williams 2013

riskFactors: high-speed-running spikes (or ABSENCE — unexposed hamstrings fail on the rare maximal sprint)
warningSigns: reduced sprint confidence / not reaching top speed
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Nordic 2x/week building doses (off/pre-season); 1x/week maintenance in-season; PLUS regular counted exposure to >95% max velocity for backs and mobile forwards
exercisesToAvoid: heavy Nordic/GHR novelty the day before matches
monitoringRecommendations: weekly Nordic force or bridge-hold check
high-speed-running exposure counting (GPS or session RPE proxy)
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Attwood 2018 (rugby movement-control RCT); Brooks 2006 (rugby hamstring epidemiology); van Dyk 2019 (Nordic meta, ~50%)

warningSigns: instability or high-ankle pain on push-off and rotation
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: balance/proprioception 3x/week for 6+ months post-sprain; calf capacity year-round
exercisesToAvoid: reactive cutting + contact volume immediately after a sprain
loaded rotation on a symptomatic high ankle
monitoringRecommendations: single-leg balance checks after any sprain

warningSigns: loss of neutral-spine control under load
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: trunk-stiffness work 2-3x/week; hip + thoracic mobility daily; manage weekly axial-loading volume
exercisesToAvoid: stacking heavy axial loading on scrum-heavy weeks
monitoringRecommendations: axial-load volume tracking across gym + scrummaging
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Williams 2013; expert consensus (rugby S&C on axial-load management)

decisionRules.then: gym is CNS priming only (a few jumps/activation drills) or rest; no strength development

remove heavy axial-loading and high-soreness work (heavy squat/deadlift, Nordic/GHR building doses, new exercises); keep only familiar low-fatigue maintenance — rugby's collision recovery is slower than non-contact sport
decisionRules.source: post-match recovery kinetics in collision sport (Naughton 2020); DOMS/taper consensus

decisionRules.then: cut gym volume ~50%; maintenance micro-doses only; recovery leads — collision load compounds and injury risk rises through congested blocks
decisionRules.source: Cross 2016 (match congestion and injury risk in professional rugby)

decisionRules.then: force a deload week: cap volume, protect availability, flag for review — spikes in collision + running load elevate injury risk
decisionRules.source: Gabbett 2016 (training-injury prevention paradox; collision-load context) — methodology contested, used conservatively

decisionRules.then: rebuild gradually — one step down from planned load; no spikes; the return-to-contact window is high-risk

decisionRules.if: readiness score low (poor sleep + soreness + low wellness)
decisionRules.then: autoregulate down one step; quality over volume; do not test
treat as neuromuscular fatigue: reduce CNS-demanding work; recheck in 48 h — especially after heavy collision matches
withhold training until symptom-free; resume gradually

hold strength at minimal effective volume (1-2 short heavy sessions/week) — but neck + shoulder + hamstring prehab are NON-NEGOTIABLE weekly items; dropping them in-season is when the collision injuries they mitigate occur
decisionRules.source: Rønnestad & Mujika 2014 (in-season maintenance); Hrysomallis 2016 + Attwood 2018 (prehab rationale)

decisionRules.if: high hamstring soreness or Nordic strength drop
decisionRules.then: remove maximal sprint work + heavy eccentric hamstring loading; isometric substitutes; flag — never sprint through a hamstring warning
decisionRules.source: Attwood 2018; Timmins 2016 (eccentric strength monitoring); expert consensus

decisionRules.if: high neck or shoulder soreness (post-heavy-scrum or high-tackle match)
decisionRules.then: reduce overhead + heavy pressing/lifting load; keep light isometric neck/cuff maintenance; flag for review
decisionRules.source: expert consensus (rugby S&C on cervical/shoulder load management)

decisionRules.then: reduce intensity one step on arrival days; mobility + easy work

acwr.model: acute (7-day) : chronic (28-day) workload ratio; rolling/EWMA preferred; track collision count and high-speed running as their own streams where possible
acwr.source: Gabbett 2016 — methodology contested; used as a conservative guardrail; collision-load context in rugby

loadManagement.weeklyProgressionGuideline: Avoid >~10-15% week-to-week spikes, ESPECIALLY in collision volume and high-speed running; progress ONE stressor at a time (pitch/contact volume, gym load, or sprint exposure — never all at once). Maintain regular controlled exposure to >95% max velocity for backs — under-exposure is itself a hamstring risk.

gymVolumeRanges.offSeason: high (3-4 sessions; heavy strength + robustness volume)
gymVolumeRanges.inSeason: low-moderate maintenance (2 sessions; heavy but low volume) + non-negotiable neck/shoulder/hamstring prehab

loadManagement.minimumEffectiveVolume: ~1-2 heavy low-volume sessions/week sustain strength in-season; the neck + hamstring prehab pillars survive even zero-equipment weeks (bands and a partner)
loadManagement.maximumAdaptiveVolume: Off-season is the strength-development window — push volume there, not into a collision-heavy season.
loadManagement.maximumRecoverableVolume: Constrained by collision + pitch load and (for amateurs) life load; the gym never compromises the next match or the player's contact recovery.
loadManagement.deloadRecommendations: Planned deload every 3-5 weeks in development phases; automatic deload on ACWR/readiness triggers; congested fixture weeks ARE deload weeks for the gym.
loadManagement.progressionRules: Progress load when reps/quality are met at target RPE and readiness is green.
loadManagement.regressionRules: On red readiness, high collision load or congested fixtures, drop one step (volume first, intensity second).
loadManagement.missedSessionRules: Never stack missed sessions; resume the planned wave. A missed prehab pillar (neck/hamstring/shoulder) is rescheduled within the week, not skipped.
loadManagement.source: Gabbett 2016; Cross 2016 (congestion); Rønnestad & Mujika 2014; expert consensus

factors.name: Hours since last match (collision recovery)

thresholds.modifier: no heavy axial-loading gym; recovery or activation only — collision damage peaks and lingers
moderate loads acceptable if wellness is green

factors.source: Naughton 2020 (post-match recovery in rugby: slower kinetics with collision load)

thresholds.modifier: no contact and no training until cleared; follow the World Rugby GRTP protocol (clinician-led)
corroborating signal only — never sole driver

readinessModel.notes: Subjective wellness + time-since-match (collision recovery) + sleep lead; objective signals corroborate. Suspected concussion overrides everything and is clinician-governed. Raw vitals stay private to the athlete — the coach sees only the derived readiness state and availability.

coachDashboard.principle: Coach sees DERIVED and availability signals only — never an individual's raw vitals (HRV, sleep, resting HR).
mostUsefulKpis: congestion response (did gym volume actually drop in 2-match weeks)
mostUsefulAlerts: hamstring flag on a high-sprint-exposure back
coachDashboard.trafficLightIndicators: Per-player green/amber/red from derived readiness + load state (never raw vitals).
coachDashboard.privacyNote: All per-athlete entries are DERIVED (readiness score, load state, availability, GRTP status). Raw HRV/sleep/RHR never appear on a coach surface — see TEAM-ARCHITECTURE data-isolation rules.

educationTips: why neck strength is your own contribution to lowering head-injury risk
why the Nordic is the closest thing sport science has to a hamstring vaccine
why rugby needs heavier lifting than most sports — strength IS contact currency
why collision recovery is slower than running recovery, so gym flexes around matches
why the best ability is availability

strongEvidence: Nordic hamstring programmes reduce hamstring injury (~50% incidence with adherence; L1 — van Dyk 2019)
a rugby-specific movement-control exercise programme (Activate-style) reduces injury (L1-L2 — Attwood 2018; Hislop 2017)
maximal strength and power discriminate playing level in professional rugby (L2-L3 — Argus 2012; Duthie 2003)
subjective wellness is a sensitive readiness input (L1 — Saw 2016)
in-season low-volume strength maintenance works (L2 — Rønnestad & Mujika 2014)
concussion is the most common match injury and prior concussion is the dominant risk factor (L2 — Williams 2013)
weakEvidence: neck strength as concussion protection (biologically plausible, modifiable, but causal protective evidence is emerging — Hrysomallis 2016)
the precise 50% congested-week gym-volume cut (direction certain from Cross 2016, magnitude consensus)
position-specific demand splits below professional level
areasRequiringExpertJudgement: balancing collision load, pitch load and gym load in congested periods
cervical-conditioning dose across positions (front row vs backs)
managing return to CONTACT (distinct from return to running) after injury
collision-load quantification without GPS/accelerometry at amateur level
areasRequiringFutureResearch: causal effect of neck strengthening on concussion incidence (not just head-acceleration attenuation)
collision-load thresholds for youth and amateur players
long-term brain-health implications of cumulative head-impact exposure
artificial turf vs grass injury interaction in rugby
potentialRisksIfMisimplemented: treating neck strengthening as a substitute for tackle-technique coaching or the GRTP protocol (it is an adjunct, never a treatment)
returning a player to contact before completing the World Rugby GRTP protocol
introducing Nordic/GHR at full dose in-season (the soreness injures the week, not the muscle)
stacking heavy axial-loading gym work on top of a high-collision week
treating rugby recovery like a non-contact sport — collision recovery is slower
chasing hypertrophy past the point mass costs repeat-effort speed

performanceScore.philosophy: Reflects progress toward rugby's demands — maximal strength and power for contact, the repeat-effort engine, and the robustness pillars — weighted to reward the behaviours that keep a player available across a collision-heavy season.

components.rationale: Neck/shoulder/hamstring prehab is the availability spine of a collision sport.
Strength is rugby's contact and acceleration currency.
Sustainable loading beats heroic spikes, doubly so with collision load.
The repeat-effort engine — rugby's conditioning benchmark.
The decisive action into and out of contact.
